extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning plane and projective geometry (advanced high-school/undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and worked constructions in inversion and projective geometry: definitions (projective transformations, cross-ratio, points at infinity), key theorems (Desargues, harmonic division), and constructive applications (Apollonius problem via inversion, construction of harmonic conjugates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of angle under inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under inversion, angles are preserved: two circles or lines that are orthogonal (intersect at right angles) remain orthogonal after inversion; two circles that are tangent (intersect at angle zero) remain tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: orthogonal circles map to orthogonal images; tangent circles map to tangent images. This property is used repeatedly to deduce geometric relations after inversion (illustrated with figures showing orthogonal circle systems and tangent-circle systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping of family of circles through center to lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A family of all circles passing through the center of inversion O and another fixed point A is transformed by inversion into a family of straight lines radiating from A', the image of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to translate between circle-based configurations and line-based configurations (figures referenced). The images of circles through the center become straight lines through the image point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circles tangent at center map to parallel lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A family of circles tangent to each other at the center of inversion become a system of parallel lines after inversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: the images of those circles are straight lines which do not intersect because original circles met only at the center. This observation is used in constructive transformations (see Figure 02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inversion to solve the Problem of Apollonius
rubrics_metrics.description: By inverting with respect to a suitable center, the Apollonius problem for three given circles can be transformed into an equivalent problem for three other circles; choose an equivalent triple making the problem trivial and invert back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive recipe given: (1) possibly increase radii uniformly (see next criterion) to simplify; (2) replace given circles so two are tangent at K; (3) invert about K so two circles become parallel lines b and c and the third becomes circle a; (4) the unknown circle maps to u which touches a, b, c; its radius r = half the distance between b and c; center O' is intersection of the midline between b and c with the circle about A1 of radius r + s (s is radius of a); (5) invert u to get the desired Apollonius circle (center 0 is inverse of the point inverse to K in u). Figures and intermediate steps are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform radius-increase invariance in Apollonius constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the radii of the three given circles are increased by the same quantity d, then a circle with the same center O and radius p - d will solve the new problem (where p was original solution radius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation is used to replace a given triple of circles by another triple more convenient for inversion-based solution; it allows shifting problems by uniform radius changes to obtain constructible configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated reflections and repeated inversion behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated reflections in multiple mirrors or repeated inversion in pairs/triples of circles produce infinite sequences of images with particular limiting behavior: concentric sequences, one tending to infinity and another concentrating at the center; with two external circles the images shrink until they narrow to two points (mutually inverse with respect to both circles); with three circles complex patterns arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: rectangular room (infinite images), three mirrors (special tessellation cases), two concentric circular mirrors (infinite concentric images), two external circles (images shrink to mutually inverse points), three circles (beautiful patterns). These phenomena highlight qualitative behavior of iterative transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of geometrical properties by invariance under transformation classes (Erlanger program)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical theorems can be classified according to which class of transformations they remain true under; the geometry associated with a class of transformations consists of properties invariant under that class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: metric geometry = invariant under rigid motions (congruence); similarity geometry = invariant under similarity; projective geometry = invariant under projective transformations. This viewpoint organizes geometry by transformation groups and motivates the study of projective invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and group property of projective transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: A projective transformation is any mapping realizable by a central or parallel projection, or by a finite succession of such projections. The class of projective transformations forms a group: composition and inverses remain in the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projective geometry consists of propositions unaffected by arbitrary projective transformations. Remarks about group notion: closure under composition and inverses; some technical exceptional cases (parallelism) are handled later with ideal elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidence, collinearity, and concurrence invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: Under projective transformations: points map to points, straight lines to straight lines; incidence (point on a line), collinearity (three or more points on a line), and concurrence (three or more lines through a point) are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: properties such as 'triangle' are projective but properties involving lengths or angles (e.g., 'equilateral') are not. Use incidence invariance to derive many projective results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desargues's Theorem (projective formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles ABC and A'B'C' are placed so that lines joining corresponding vertices are concurrent at point O, then the intersections of corresponding sides (extended) are three collinear points. The converse (collinear intersections imply concurrency of joining-vertex lines) also holds in appropriate cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is projective in nature; proof can be given by viewing the plane figure as the projection of a space configuration (perspective from a point). Note distinction: proving Desargues purely in the plane requires similarity notions (metric), whereas the space proof uses only incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and invariance of the cross-ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: For four collinear points A,B,C,D the cross-ratio (ABCD) is defined as (CA/DA) / (CB/DB) (with directed lengths); this signed cross-ratio is invariant under central and parallel projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches: use triangle area relations (central projection) or similar triangles (parallel projection). Coordinate formula given: (ABCD) = ((x3-x1)(x4-x2))/((x3-x2)(x4-x1)) with directed coordinates. Cross-ratio depends on order; sign indicates separation of point pairs. Invariance is central to projective geometry and can be extended to lines and planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic division and harmonic conjugates
rubrics_metrics.description: When the cross-ratio (ABCD) = -1, points C and D divide segment AB internally and externally in the same ratio; C and D are harmonic conjugates of each other with respect to A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric significance: harmonic division is an important projective configuration. Construction methods (e.g., using complete quadrilateral) and special properties are discussed in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation identities of the cross-ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Permuting the order of four collinear points yields at most six distinct cross-ratio values: X, 1 - X, 1/X, 1/(1 - X), (X - 1)/X, (X/(X - 1)) (text gives examples X, 1 - X, 1/X and remarks on harmonic case X = -1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: there are 24 orderings yielding only six distinct numerical cross-ratio values; some coincide in special cases (e.g., harmonic division).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ratio for concurrent lines and coaxial planes
rubrics_metrics.description: The cross-ratio can be defined for four coplanar concurrent lines as the cross-ratio of their intersections with any other line in the plane, or by formula using sines: (12 3 4) = (sin(1,3)/sin(1,4)) / (sin(2,3)/sin(2,4)) with sign determined by separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, define cross-ratio for four coaxial planes by intersecting with a line or a fifth plane. Invariance under projective transformations extends to these configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective correspondence (biunique, cross-ratio preserving)
rubrics_metrics.description: A biunique correspondence between points of two lines that preserves the cross-ratio of every set of four points is called a projective correspondence; any such correspondence can be realized by at most two projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction facts/exercises: given an arbitrary projective correspondence between two lines, one can shift one line so the correspondence arises from a single projection; more generally any finite succession of projections between two lines can be replaced by two projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete quadrilateral harmonic property
rubrics_metrics.description: In a complete quadrilateral (four lines, no three concurrent, with their six intersection points), take a diagonal AB and let C and D be its intersections with the other two diagonals; then (ABCD) = -1, i.e., those intersections separate A and B harmonically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses successive projections and cross-ratio invariance: (ABCD) = (IFHD) by projection from E, = (BACD) by projection from G, leading to x = 1/x hence x = -1. Practical consequence: one can construct the harmonic conjugate D of a given point C on AB using straightedge alone by constructing a suitable complete quadrilateral (explicit construction algorithm given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Points at infinity (ideal points) and line at infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid exceptional cases involving parallel lines, extend each line by adding a single ideal point (the point at infinity determined by the family of parallel lines) and add a single ideal line (the line at infinity) containing all ideal points. With these conventions every pair of lines intersects in a single point and through any two points one and only one line may be drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: adding one ideal point per line (not two) preserves uniqueness of line through two points; the ideal line is necessary to have the unique line through two ideal points. This formal simplification removes exceptional-case handling in projective constructions and allows projection arguments to be stated uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ideal elements to streamline projection arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing points and lines at infinity enables a uniform treatment of projection (central and parallel) and removes the need to treat parallelism as a separate exceptional case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuitive justification: as a line is rotated toward parallelism, intersection points 'recede to infinity'; formally adding ideal points/line allows incidence laws to hold in the extended domain and simplifies theorems and constructions. The text begins applying this to projections of planes onto planes (continued beyond the chunk).
